analysis.one_liner: Requires public companies to fully disclose executive pay, put it to a shareholder vote, and claw back pay tied to fraud.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it sat in the House Financial Services Committee and its subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced publicly traded companies to tell shareholders, in plain terms, what their top executives are paid — including pensions, perks, and bonuses triggered by a merger or sale. It would have required a separate shareholder vote to approve executive pay packages and golden parachutes, and would have required executives to pay back bonuses received before an accounting restatement or tied to fraud.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders — including ordinary people whose retirement savings are invested in mutual funds and pensions — would get a clear picture of what top executives take out of the companies they own stakes in, and a vote on it. Workers and the public would also gain visibility into the gap between executive pay and the performance measures companies claim to use.

how_it_helps.text: Companies must publish a comprehensive statement of executive compensation — including accrued pension value, other benefits, and any side agreements — in annual reports and proxy materials.
Executive pay plans and golden parachute arrangements would each require a separate shareholder vote, giving owners of the company a say on pay for the first time.

Executives would have to reimburse their company for bonuses received within 18 months before a negative accounting restatement, pay tied to performance measures they failed to meet, or compensation related to fraud.
Compensation disclosures filed electronically must appear in a clear, simple, and readily accessible format, rather than dense legal filings.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded companies and their top executives, who would face new disclosure requirements, shareholder votes on their pay, and the possibility of clawbacks — plus compliance costs for preparing the simpler, more complete filings.

drawbacks.text: Public companies would bear new compliance costs to prepare detailed compensation statements, separate shareholder votes, and simpler-format filings, and the SEC would need to write the required rules within one year of enactment.
The bill does not specify what happens if shareholders vote down a compensation plan, so the say-on-pay requirement's real bite would depend on rules the SEC later writes.
Disclosure alone does not cap executive pay; well-paid executives and boards could still negotiate large packages as long as they describe them clearly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are transparency and accountability for shareholders who currently must untangle opaque filings to learn what executives earn, and the ability to claw back pay tied to fraud or missed performance targets. The costs are real but modest: compliance work for public companies and rule-writing for the SEC. This is the same policy direction Congress eventually adopted in later years, suggesting the design was workable; the main limitation is that disclosure and votes inform shareholders rather than directly limiting pay levels.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, and neither held any action on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Barney Frank and five other senior House Democrats introduced the bill on November 10, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
On January 5, 2006, the committee referred it to its Subcommittee on Capital Markets, Insurance and Government Sponsored Enterprises.
No further action — no subcommittee vote, no full committee markup, no floor vote — appears in the record before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
The bill drew 33 cosponsors: 32 Democrats and 1 Independent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives of large public companies came out ahead: they avoided the new disclosure requirements, shareholder votes on their pay, and clawback rules. Shareholders, whose retirement savings depend on how corporate profits are divided, did not get the transparency the bill promised.

for.name: Rep. Barney Frank
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled five senior committee and subcommittee chairs as original cosponsors.

for.name: 33 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. George Miller, Obey, Rangel, Sabo, and Velazquez as original cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to the Capital Markets subcommittee, and never held a markup or reported it out.

against.name: Michael Oxley
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before his committee for consideration during the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on the bill; no roll-call votes occurred.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their top executives
industries.note: The bill requires full disclosure of executive pay, shareholder votes on pay packages and golden parachutes, and repayment of bonuses tied to fraud, missed targets, or pre-restatement accounting. Executives' interest in keeping pay arrangements opaque runs against shareholders' interest in knowing what they pay for.

New disclosure formats, SEC rulemaking, and clawback policies would have generated compliance work for outside counsel and proxy preparers, while simplification rules could have reduced some filing complexity.
